chunks: And from him, from Ahmad ibn Idris, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Abd al-Rahman ibn Abi Najran, from Asim ibn Humayd, from Muhammad ibn Qays, from Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him), who said:

The Commander of the Faithful (peace be upon him) ruled regarding a mukatab (a slave who has contracted manumission for a specified sum) who had a free woman under him; she bequeathed to him upon her death. He said: 'The bequest of the wife to her husband is not valid, because he is a mukatab who has not yet been freed and does not inherit.'
So he ruled that he inherits according to the portion of him that has been freed, and his bequest to him is valid according to the portion of him that has been freed.
And he ruled regarding a mukatab who had paid a quarter of what was due to him, and he was bequeathed to; so he validated for him a quarter of the bequest.

And he ruled regarding a free man who bequeathed to his mukatabah (female slave under contract), and she had paid a sixth of what was due to her; so he validated for her according to the portion of her that had been freed.
And he ruled regarding the bequest of a mukatab who had paid part of what he was contracted to pay, that it is validated from his bequest according to the portion of him that has been freed.

key_terms.أَمِيرُ الْمُؤْمِنِينَ: The Commander of the Faithful, a title referring to Imam Ali (peace be upon him).
key_terms.مُكَاتَب: A slave who has entered into a contract with their master to pay a specific sum for their manumission.

ai.seo_question: How does Islamic law determine the inheritance share of a slave who has contracted for their freedom (mukatab)?
ai.summary: This hadith from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam* elucidates the juristic principle of proportional manumission (*nisab al-ta'abbud*), where Imam Ali (AS) ruled that a *mukatab*'s capacity to inherit and receive bequests is strictly limited to the fraction of their freedom already purchased. This ruling distinguishes the *mukatab* from a fully free person (*hurra*) or a slave (*abd*), ensuring that their legal rights in estate distribution reflect their partial status as free individuals. It highlights the Shia scholarly emphasis on precise quantitative application of Quranic inheritance laws to transitional legal statuses.
